title: Math and Science: Chance, Tests, and Tallies
objectives: I can use ten words to talk about chance, tests, and data.
I can explain what probability, likelihood, and chance tell us.
I can describe an experiment using trial, tally, average, and cluster.
I can write about an experiment I could run, using words from this unit.
rationale: Fifth-grade math and science ask students to run tests, collect data, and talk about what is likely. The vocabulary for this work is scattered across both subjects: probability and experiment are the two named content terms; tally, average, trial, and cluster name what students do with data; and chance, uncertain, random, and likelihood name the ideas about what might happen. Three of the words (average, trial, cluster) have strong everyday senses that students must learn to separate from the science and math sense. The passage is a class coin-flip experiment, which lets every word appear in a concrete, safe setting with true statements about chance. Proof, research, excerpt, and logical return because a good experiment needs logic, a written record, and honest limits on what the evidence shows.

words.def: A number that tells how likely it is that something will happen.
words.ex: The probability of rolling a six on a fair die is one in six.
words.ex2: There is a high probability of snow tonight, so the school may close.
words.nonExample: A guess without any numbers is not a probability.
words.rel: how likely something is, as a number

apps.academic: Mathematicians measure probability with numbers between zero and one.
apps.spoken: What's the probability that it will rain on Friday?
apps.writing: Use probability when you give a number for how likely an event is.

cloze.s: If two of ten marbles in the bag are red, the ___ of picking a red marble is two out of ten.

cloze2.s: The weather report said the ___ of rain was ninety percent, so we packed umbrellas.

misuse.s: The probability of rolling a seven on a standard six-sided die is very high.
misuse.why: A standard die has only the numbers one to six, so rolling a seven is impossible.

visual.alt: A die beside a bar chart.

words.def: A test done to learn something or to try out an idea.
words.ex: For our experiment, we dropped balls from different heights to see how high they bounced.
words.ex2: The scientist repeated the experiment three times to make sure the result was not an accident.
words.nonExample: Reading about a topic in a book is not an experiment.
words.rel: a test to find out something

apps.academic: A fair experiment changes only one thing at a time.
apps.spoken: We did an experiment with plants in science.
apps.writing: Use experiment for a planned test that answers a question.

cloze.s: Our science ___ tested whether plants grow taller in sunlight or in shade.

cloze2.s: To learn which paper towel holds the most water, the class set up an ___ with four brands.

misuse.s: The experiment was a story the class read aloud, and nothing was tested.
misuse.why: An experiment is a planned test; reading a story is not an experiment.

words.frame: In my experiment, I would test ___.

words.def: To count up and keep a record of marks or results.
words.ex: After the vote, the teacher began to tally the ballots at her desk.
words.ex2: Maya would tally each bird she saw at the feeder and then add the marks at the end of the day.
words.nonExample: Guessing how many birds visited without recording them is not to tally.

apps.academic: Scientists tally their observations so they can compare days or places.
apps.writing: Use tally to describe counting and recording each result as it happens.

cloze.s: We kept a chart to ___ how many students walked, rode a bike, or took the bus to school.

cloze2.s: After the game, the judges began to ___ the points for each team on a large board.

misuse.s: To tally the votes, she threw them away without counting any of them.
misuse.why: To tally is to count and record; throwing votes away is not tallying.

visual.alt: A hand marking tally lines on a chart.

words.def: The number you get by adding values and dividing by how many there are.

senses.def: Ordinary or typical; neither very high nor very low.
senses.example: It was an average day, with nothing special happening.

words.ex2: Our class average on the math quiz was eighty-five points.
words.nonExample: The biggest number in a list is not the average.
words.rel: the middle value from adding and dividing

apps.academic: Scientists use the average of many measurements to get a more reliable result.
apps.spoken: What's the average temperature in July?
apps.writing: Use average for the sum of numbers divided by how many numbers there are.

cloze.s: To find the ___ of our five test scores, we added them up and divided by five.

cloze2.s: The ___ rainfall in April was three inches, found by adding each year's amount and dividing by ten.

misuse.s: The average of 2, 4, and 6 is 12 because 2 plus 4 plus 6 is 12 and we do not divide.
misuse.why: An average is the sum divided by how many numbers there are, so the average of 2, 4, and 6 is 4.

visual.alt: A balance scale next to a division sign.

words.def: A possibility that something will happen.
words.ex: There is a good chance of rain this afternoon.
words.ex2: The coin has an equal chance of landing on heads or tails.
words.nonExample: A sure thing is not a chance.

apps.academic: Scientists talk about the chance of an event, such as a storm or a flood.
apps.writing: Use chance for how possible something is, often with words like good or small.

cloze.s: With dark clouds and thunder in the distance, there was a good ___ of rain by lunch.

cloze2.s: Because the game was close, each team had an equal ___ of winning in the final minute.

misuse.s: The chance that a dropped ball will fall upward is very good.
misuse.why: A dropped ball falls down, so there is no real chance that it falls upward.

visual.alt: A spinning wheel next to a clover.

words.frame: There is a good chance that ___.

words.def: Not sure; not able to know what will happen.
words.ex: The weather was so unsettled that the picnic plans were uncertain.
words.ex2: She felt uncertain about the answer and checked the book again.
words.nonExample: A fact that everyone has checked is not uncertain.

apps.academic: Scientists say an outcome is uncertain when they cannot yet predict it.
apps.writing: Use uncertain for a person who is unsure, or an outcome that cannot be known yet.

cloze.s: It was ___ whether the game would go on, since dark clouds were still moving over the field.

cloze2.s: The new student felt ___ about which table to sit at, so she stood by the door.

misuse.s: Because everyone checked the answer, it was uncertain and no one could tell if it was right.
misuse.why: If everyone checked the answer, it is certain, not uncertain.

visual.alt: A line from certain to uncertain, with uncertain near the doubtful end.

words.def: Happening by chance, with no plan or pattern.
words.ex: The teacher drew a random name from the hat to choose the next speaker.
words.ex2: A random pattern of dots covered the page, with no two dots lined up.
words.nonExample: A schedule that repeats every Monday is not random.

apps.academic: Scientists use random samples so that every member of a group has an equal chance.
apps.writing: Use random for a choice or event that has no plan behind it.

cloze.s: To be fair, the coach picked players in ___ order by drawing numbers from a bag.

cloze2.s: The spinner stopped on a ___ color each time, with no way to know which one was next.

misuse.s: The teacher used a random method by picking the same student every day.
misuse.why: A random method has no pattern; picking the same student each day is a pattern.

visual.alt: A die beside crossing arrows showing a mixed-up order.

words.def: One try at a test; one run of an experiment.

senses.def: A court case where a judge or jury decides if someone is guilty.
senses.example: The trial lasted three days before the jury returned its verdict.

words.ex: In each trial, the toy car rolled down the ramp while the class timed it.
words.ex2: After the third trial, the results were nearly the same as the first two.
words.nonExample: Watching the experiment from the doorway is not a trial.

apps.academic: Scientists run many trials to see if the result is steady.
apps.spoken: We did ten trials with the ball.
apps.writing: Use trial for one try or run of a test.

cloze.s: On the fourth ___, the plant grew two centimeters, a little more than in the first three.

cloze2.s: The class repeated the ___ with a new ball to see whether the bounce would change.

misuse.s: Each trial was a lunch menu that listed what students would eat.
misuse.why: A trial is one try of a test, not a menu.

visual.alt: A flask with a circular arrow.

words.def: A group of things close together.

senses.example: Penguins cluster in tight groups to stay warm.

words.ex: A cluster of bright stars lit up the corner of the sky.
words.ex2: On the dot plot, a cluster of points appeared around the number nine.
words.nonExample: A single star far from all the others is not a cluster.

apps.academic: In data, a cluster of values shows that many results are close together.
apps.spoken: A cluster of grapes hung on the vine.
apps.writing: Use cluster for a group close together, such as stars, dots, or grapes.

cloze.s: On the graph, a ___ of dots near the middle showed that most results were alike.

cloze2.s: A ___ of berries hung from the branch, so the birds came to eat them all.

misuse.s: A cluster is a single object standing far away from every other object.
misuse.why: A cluster is a group close together, not a single object far from others.

visual.alt: A bunch of grapes and a star.

words.def: How probable it is that something will happen.
words.ex: The likelihood of snow is high because the temperature is below freezing.
words.ex2: With thick clouds overhead, the likelihood of rain by evening was great.
words.nonExample: A guaranteed event is not a matter of likelihood.

apps.academic: Forecasters describe the likelihood of storms with percentages.
apps.spoken: What's the likelihood of a pop quiz?
apps.writing: Use likelihood for how probable an outcome is, in words or numbers.

cloze.s: With ice on the road, the ___ of an accident was high, so the driver slowed down.

cloze2.s: Because the team had lost every game, the ___ of a win this week seemed small.

misuse.s: The likelihood of an event that cannot happen is very high.
misuse.why: The likelihood of an impossible event is zero, not high.

visual.alt: A line from impossible to certain, with likelihood measured between.

passage.title: Flipping for Answers
paras: Does a coin land on heads exactly half the time? Mr. Singh's class decided to find out with an experiment. They knew that a fair coin has a probability of one half for heads, but they were uncertain about what would happen in a small number of flips. "Every flip is random," he said. "No one can predict a single result."

Each pair of students completed twenty trials. One partner flipped the coin, and the other kept a tally of the results on a chart, marking every head and tail. "A tally keeps the count clear," said Lena. "We can add it up later."

When the pairs posted their results, the class noticed that few pairs got exactly ten heads. Most results formed a cluster between eight and twelve. Lena found the average number of heads for the whole class, and it was close to ten. "The chance of heads is one half," she said, "but a small experiment can still surprise you."

Mr. Singh explained that the likelihood of seeing a result close to one half rises as the number of trials grows. "With a thousand flips, the share of heads usually gets closer to half," he said. The class decided to combine all of their trials and test his idea.

qs.q: In paragraph 2, the word "trial" most nearly means
choices: one try or run of the experiment
a court case about a coin
qs.why: Each pair completed twenty trials, flipping the coin twenty times, so a trial is one try of the experiment.

qs.q: What does the author mean when the results "formed a cluster" between eight and twelve?
choices: The results were spread out over every number.
Most results grouped close together between eight and twelve.
The pairs argued over the numbers.
The results were all exactly ten.
qs.why: A cluster is a group close together, and most pairs had between eight and twelve heads.

qs.q: Which detail shows that a single coin flip is random?
choices: Mr. Singh says no one can predict a single result.
qs.why: Mr. Singh says every flip is random and no one can predict a single result.

qs.q: Why does Lena say a small experiment can still surprise you?
choices: With few flips, the results may not match one half exactly.
The class did not keep a tally.
qs.why: Few pairs got exactly ten heads, so a small number of flips can give results that differ from the expected one half.

qs.q: Which sentence best states the main idea of the passage?
choices: More trials usually give results closer to what probability predicts.
qs.why: The class sees surprises in small experiments, and Mr. Singh explains that more trials usually bring the share of heads closer to half.

teacher.overview: Students learn ten words for experiments, data, and chance: probability and experiment as the two named content terms, tally, average, trial, and cluster for working with data, and chance, uncertain, random, and likelihood for ideas about what might happen. The passage is a class coin-flip experiment with true statements about probability. Writing asks students to design and describe a small experiment.

notes.va.probability.n: Probability is a number, from zero to one or zero to one hundred percent, that tells how likely something is. Students often say probability when they mean possibility; probability has a number. Use a spinner or a bag of marbles to show it.
notes.va.experiment.n: An experiment is a test used to learn something. Students may think an experiment is only for science; it can also be a math or art test. Link to research from unit 16: an experiment is research you do yourself. Ask what question the experiment answers.
notes.va.tally.v: Tally is a verb meaning to count and record marks, and also a noun for the count. Teach tally marks in groups of five. Ask students to tally something in the room and then say the total in a sentence.
notes.va.average.n: Average here is the number you get by adding values and dividing by how many there are. Students also use average to mean ordinary, so show both. Calculate an average from five test scores together.
notes.va.chance.n: Chance means the possibility that something will happen. It can also mean an opportunity, as in a chance to win. Teach the possibility sense and mention the other. Link to probability: chance is the everyday word, probability the math word.
notes.va.uncertain.adj: Uncertain means not sure, and it is the opposite of certain. It can describe a person or an outcome. Have students sort events into certain, likely, uncertain, unlikely, and impossible.
notes.va.random.adj: Random means by chance, with no plan or pattern. Students use random to mean strange, as in random comments; teach the math sense first. Show a random draw from a hat and compare with a pattern.
notes.va.trial.n: Trial has an experiment sense, one try, and a legal sense, a court case. The passage uses the first. Tell students the second so they are not surprised. Ask how many trials the class ran and why.
notes.va.cluster.n: Cluster is a group of things close together, and it can also be a verb. In data, a cluster of dots shows many values near each other. Show a dot plot and have students circle the cluster.
notes.va.likelihood.n: Likelihood is how probable it is that something will happen. It is a bit more formal than chance. Students can compare words on a likelihood ladder from impossible to certain. Pair with probability.

teacher.model: Think-aloud: 'The class flipped a coin twenty times in each pair. That one flip is a trial, one try of the experiment. They kept a tally so they would not lose count. Most results clustered near ten, so the dots on a graph would pile up in the middle. The class average was close to ten, which is what the probability of one half predicts.'
discuss: Which of the ten words is closest to the idea of how sure we can be?
Which of these words would you use in a science report, and which in a math lesson?
misconceptions: If the probability is one half, every pair of flips will give exactly half heads.
A trial is only a court case.
Chance and probability are exactly the same.
extend: Run a class experiment with a spinner, tally the results, and graph the cluster.
Write a probability story about a day when everything was uncertain.
Compare the average of the class's results to the average of the whole school's results.
teacher.reviewAdvice: Revisit proof, research, excerpt, and logical by asking students what proof their experiment gives, how they would research the question, how they would quote an excerpt from a lab note, and why a logical plan matters. Return to the ten words after two days, again at one week, using a new experiment.

frames: Most results formed a cluster near ___.
wida.oral: Partner A describes a small experiment and the number of trials. Partner B tells what to tally, predicts the likelihood of one result, and says whether the outcome is certain or uncertain.

needsReview: Statements about probability (a fair coin has probability one half for heads; with more flips the share of heads tends to come closer to half) are standard and true but simplified; the passage's class experiment is invented.

Spanish glosses not reviewed by a native speaker: probabilidad is used for both probability and likelihood; posibilidad (chance), promedio (average), aleatorio (random), prueba (trial; ensayo is also common), grupo (cluster), contar (tally; llevar la cuenta is also used).

Teacher notes mention secondary senses (average as ordinary, chance as opportunity, trial as court case, random as odd) that are standard dictionary senses but were not checked against a cited dictionary.
